entry.title: Pietro Miotti's AI Agents Rediscover Maya Site Using NASA Lidar Data
entry.content:

Technologist and traveler Pietro Miotti deployed a network of AI agents to analyze NASA lidar data of Mexican jungles, resulting in the rediscovery of an unmapped Classic-period Maya civic center within 72 hours. The agents processed approximately 1,200 square kilometers of jungle canopy data to identify structured anomalies, flagging a clifftop site featuring a plaza, a pyramid, a courtyard, and a potential reservoir.

After Miotti submitted a formal report detailing the findings to Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History, officials confirmed the coordinates did not match their active register, though subsequent literature checks revealed professional archaeologists had independently mapped the same location. Miotti notes the exercise demonstrates how autonomous agents can lower barriers to geographic and archaeological exploration by automating visual analysis of remote survey data.

Research involving 100,000 participants from the NIH All of Us Research Program indicates that nearly all individuals carry genetic variants that affect medication response. The study found that 99.5% of participants have at least one relevant variant, and approximately 24% have taken medications, such as statins or acid-reducing drugs, that are directly influenced by their genetics.

These findings highlight the potential for pharmacogenomics to enhance precision medicine through optimized drug selection and dosing. However, researchers note that genetic testing is not yet routine clinical practice due to a lack of diverse population data, insufficient clinical guidelines, and the complicating effects of age and organ function on drug metabolism.

entry.title: Heinz von Foerster’s 1960 Doomsday Prediction Offers Lessons for Modern Scientific Forecasting
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

In 1960, physicist Heinz von Foerster and colleagues published a paper in Science predicting that global population growth would lead to "doomsday" on November 13, 2026. The prediction was intentionally engineered using a mathematical equation fitted to historical data to demonstrate that exponential growth rates were unsustainable, which subsequently fueled a wave of overpopulation alarmism and justified harmful policies such as forced sterilizations and China's one-child policy.

Decades later, as many nations confront declining birth rates and aging populations rather than overpopulation, the 1960 prediction serves as a cautionary tale about modeling limitations and the risks of blending science with advocacy. The analysis underscores that modern catastrophe predictions should be approached with humility, transparency, and rigorous scrutiny to prevent repeating past forecasting failures.

entry.title: e-means Algorithm Achieves Faster K-Means Clustering
entry.content:
Links: e-means.github.io | hacker news

The e-means project introduces an optimization method for the k-means clustering problem that combines mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages. By replacing full-batch iterations with moving averages and applying automatic hyperparameter tuning derived from scaling laws, the method matches or exceeds the clustering loss of Lloyd's algorithm in significantly fewer epochs.

Evaluated across a range of embedding and synthetic datasets, e-means delivers substantial wall-clock speedups on both CPU and GPU compared to existing implementations like Faiss and Flash-KMeans. The algorithm also incorporates a proportional split strategy to revive dead clusters and a finalization stage that reduces training loss with minimal performance overhead.

entry.title: University of Warsaw and International Team Demonstrate Room-Temperature Quantum Supersolid
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | hacker news

An international research team has demonstrated a quantum supersolid—a state of matter combining the orderly crystal structure of a solid with the frictionless flow of a superfluid—at room temperature. Rather than using ultracold atomic systems, the scientists generated hybrid quasiparticles called exciton polaritons by coupling light and matter inside an organic semiconductor and liquid-crystal microcavity.

Published in Science Advances, the findings involve collaborators from the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology, IBM Research Zurich, and CNRS. The team identified the supersolid phase by observing spontaneous symmetry breaking and regularly spaced density variations in the emitted light. The platform's ability to operate at room temperature and offer electrical tunability provides a versatile tool for exploring exotic quantum phenomena and advancing future optical computing technologies.

entry.title: Cary Institute Study Links Acorns and Mouse Populations to Lyme Disease Risk
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com

A 35-year ecological study conducted by researchers at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, reveals that white-footed mouse populations and oak tree acorn production are significantly stronger predictors of nymphal tick abundance than white-tailed deer populations. The long-term data show that heavy acorn crops provide abundant food for forest rodents, enabling mouse populations to surge and subsequently drive up nymphal tick numbers two years later.

Despite the clear link between mice and overall tick abundance, high mouse populations do not consistently predict a higher proportion of infected ticks, as other lesser-transmitting host species dilute the pathogen's prevalence within the ecosystem. Furthermore, the findings indicate that blacklegged ticks survive temperature extremes more effectively than previously assumed by sheltering in soil and leaf litter, complicating traditional assumptions about how weather and deer impact Lyme disease exposure.

entry.title: Scripps Institution of Oceanography Identifies Viscosity of Marine Snow as Carbon Transport Factor
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | hacker news

Researchers at UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln have found that the viscosity of marine snow—the sinking clumps of organic debris in the ocean—significantly affects how much carbon reaches the deep seafloor. Using 3D confocal microscopy and fluorescent molecules, the team observed that stickier, more viscous particles resist bacterial degradation longer, allowing them to transport up to six times more carbon into the deep ocean than thinner particles.

The findings, published in Science with a companion study in Nature Communications, reveal a complex microscopic landscape in ocean mucus that governs how bacteria interact with organic matter. This improved understanding of marine snow dynamics helps clarify a long-standing puzzle in the global carbon cycle and offers insights into other biological systems where bacteria encounter mucus, such as coral reefs and human digestive tracts.

The concept describes an evolutionary turning point where older animal lineages nearing extinction coexist and overlap with newer groups that are beginning to diversify, occurring independently of mass extinction events.

The findings are based on the Paja Formation's exceptionally rich Early Cretaceous marine ecosystem, which preserves surviving Jurassic lineages alongside emerging Cretaceous groups, including giant marine reptiles, turtles, and sharks. The researchers attribute this rare coexistence to favorable environmental conditions such as warm greenhouse temperatures, high sea levels, nutrient-rich coastal waters, and newly opened ocean connections between the eastern Pacific and early Atlantic.

entry.title: Paul Dirac's Mathematical Formula for Making Any Integer with Four 2s

While advanced mathematical tools like factorials, the Gamma function, and complex numbers can help solve specific numbers, physicist Paul Dirac devised a general solution that applies to any integer.

Dirac's method utilizes nested square roots and base-2 logarithms to construct a universal formula. By substituting the number 2 with the square root of 4, the approach strictly adheres to the puzzle's constraint of using four 2s, providing a systematic solution to a problem historically popular among mathematicians.

entry.title: Regensburg Center and Max Planck Institute Researchers Demonstrate Space-Time Limit for Electrons
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com

Researchers at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy and the Max Planck Institute have experimentally demonstrated a fundamental physical limit governing electron behavior, known as the space-time limit. Using ultrafast lasers and scanning tunneling microscopy, the team observed that an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision, as improving temporal resolution causes the electron's quantum wave packet to spread out spatially.

The experiments revealed that electrons moving across a microscopic gap experience a 500-attosecond delay in responding to light fields while behaving as quantum waves capable of tunneling through energy barriers. While operating ultrafast electronics at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion remains a long-term technological goal, the findings could eventually help researchers control chemical reactions and develop advanced quantum information systems.

entry.title: Study Attributes Origins of Earth's Great Unconformity to Mantle Dynamics
entry.content:

Researchers at the University of Wollongong have linked the origins of the Great Unconformity—a massive missing interval in Earth's geological record spanning over a billion years—to tectonic activity and mantle dynamics during ancient supercontinent breakups. By running global geodynamic models, the team demonstrated how mantle convection drove continental-scale uplift and subsequent weathering that sanded down exposed landmasses prior to the Cambrian period.

The study provides new insight into a decades-long geological mystery where Cambrian sandstone directly overlays basement rocks aged between 1.2 billion and 1.8 billion years. In addition to clarifying why the unconformity is best preserved in North America, the findings suggest that the same global landscape transformations helped set the stage for the rapid proliferation of complex life in Earth's ancient seas.
